### Past monitoring by INBO

From 2020 to 2024, INBO conducted camera trap-based monitoring of the Chinese muntjac within Park Vordenstein (municipality of Schoten), which hosts the longest-established Chinese muntjac population in Flanders (@sec-invasions), and the nearby forest areas Peerdsbos and De Inslag (both municipality of Brasschaat)[@dhondt_monitoring_2023; @neeckx_occurrence_2024].
Monitoring was conducted during the winter periods 2020–2021 (December to June), 2021–2022, 2022–2023, and 2023–2024 (November to May).
As muntjac prefer forest habitats with dense vegetation, visibility is maximized during winter months when leaves have dropped (@sec-biology, @sec-expert-judgement).

In total 33 camera traps were deployed:
16 were placed in Park Vordenstein and an additional camera was placed next to the corridor connecting Park Vordenstein with Peerdsbos.
These cameras remained active during all four monitoring periods.
Additionally, 16 cameras were placed in Peerdsbos during the first two study periods and moved to De Inslag during the last two study periods.
Sampling locations were chosen at random, but then (to some extent) adapted to the local habitat situation.

### Current monitoring by ANB

Again in Park Vordenstein, ANB has set up a number of so-called rapid-response cameras.
These cameras are strategically placed in locations where Chinese muntjac are known or expected to pass by (e.g., corridors connecting habitat areas or frequently used routes).
The goal here is to enable immediate management actions in response to Chinese muntjac sightings.

The cameras are equipped with a system that sends out an automatic alert when a Chinese muntjac is detected, allowing a trained hunting team to be deployed rapidly to locate and remove the animal.
Images are not collected or stored as the focus is on real-time detection and response.

### Future monitoring by INBO

Additional monitoring to be conducted by INBO is planned in the context of the project [M&M: monitoring of muntjac and catfish](https://www.vlaanderen.be/inbo/en-GB/projects/mm-monitoring-van-muntjak-en-meerval).
The following information based on internal information from Bram D'hondt, who coordinates the project on behalf of INBO.

In general, this monitoring project is aimed at supporting management of the Chinese muntjac by ANB.
For the winter season of 2025 / 2026 the primary monitoring scope is to determine the boundaries of the distribution of the Chinese muntjac population in the province of Antwerp.
The corresponding priority monitoring locations are Bergeyckse Bossen and Marum (both municipality of Brecht), were 9 cameras are placed per location from October 2025 to January 2026, and s'Herenbos (municipality of Malle) and Kalmthoutse Heide (municipality of Kalmthout), were also 9 cameras are deployed from January to May 2026.
Additional, non-primary monitoring locations lie in the provinces of Antwerp, municipality of Oud-Turnhout (Zwaneven), West-Flanders (Blankenberge), East-Flanders (Kluisbergen, Zulte), or are yet to be determined.

### Marten Network (Marternetwerk)

In the IAS expert survey conducted at INBO (@sec-expert-judgement),
the Marten Network was indicated as a monitoring initiative that can in principle pick up the Chinese muntjac.
However, the expert remarked that such pick up will be rather sporadic.

The [Marten Network](https://www.vlaanderen.be/inbo/marternetwerk/) relies on roadkill victims.
According to @maes_monitoring_2023 the project was set up in 1998 
targeting 13 carnivorous animal species (e.g., pine marten, Eurasian otter, lynx, wolf, raccoon, American mink).
Reported roadkill victims falling under the scope of the project are picked up by volunteers,
and handed over to INBO, where they are identified and autopsied to assess parameters such as age, reproduction and condition.
